steps.body:
Hand three people the same three side lengths — 4, 5 and 6 — and tell them to build a triangle. They will all build the **same** triangle.

It may be flipped or turned, but no one can produce a different shape. Three sides leave nothing to choose, which is what mathematicians mean when they say the conditions **determine a unique triangle**.
Test whether the givens leave any freedom at all.

widget.prompt: Start from SSA and switch to SSS — the criterion where all three sides are given. Then try to reveal a second, different triangle.
widget.successFeedback: No second triangle appears. With all three sides fixed there is no unresolved choice left — the shape is locked up to sliding, turning and flipping.
widget.criterionFeedback: SSA leaves a choice: the third side can swing to meet the base in two places. Choose the criterion that fixes every side.
widget.angleFeedback: The criterion is right. Now settle the angle so the construction matches the target.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Move the pieces a few more times before checking — the claim is that NO arrangement gives a second triangle.

steps.body: Not every trio of lengths works at all.
explanationVariants: 2 + 3 = 5, which is less than 6, so the two short sides cannot reach across — no triangle exists.
The two shorter sides must together exceed the longest one; 5 is not more than 6.

widget.prompt: How many triangles can be built with sides 2, 3 and 6?

options.label: None
options.feedback: 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 6. The short sides fall flat against the long one and never meet.

options.label: Exactly one
options.feedback: Check whether the sides can reach: 2 + 3 = 5, which does not span 6.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: Two triangles arise from ambiguous ANGLE conditions, never from three fixed sides.

options.label: Infinitely many
options.feedback: Fixed lengths never give infinitely many. Here they give none — the sides cannot meet.

steps.body: Two sides and the angle between them.
explanationVariants: SAS fixes both sides and the angle they enclose, so the third vertex has nowhere else to go — exactly one triangle.
The included angle removes the swing that makes SSA ambiguous.

widget.prompt: Sides of 5 and 8 with a 60° angle BETWEEN them. How many triangles?

options.label: Exactly one
options.feedback: Two sides and their included angle pin the third vertex completely — no choice remains.

options.label: None
options.feedback: These conditions are perfectly buildable; the two sides meet at 60° and the third side closes the gap.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: Two arise when the angle is NOT between the given sides. Here it is included, so the triangle is locked.

options.label: Infinitely many
options.feedback: Fixing two side lengths rules out infinitely many — the size is already set.

steps.body:
The failure case has a rule of its own. Two sides can only meet if together they are **longer** than the third.

2 and 3 cannot bridge a gap of 6: laid end to end they reach 5 and stop short. That is the triangle inequality, and it is why some lists of three lengths describe no triangle at all.
Now lock a triangle with an angle between two sides.

widget.prompt: Switch to SAS and set the included angle to 60°, then try to reveal a second valid triangle.
widget.successFeedback: SAS at 60° leaves nothing unresolved: two sides and the angle between them determine one triangle, and the second candidate collapses onto the first.
widget.criterionFeedback: SSA can branch into two different triangles. Pick the criterion whose givens remove every degree of freedom.
widget.angleFeedback: Right criterion — now set the included angle to 60° so it matches the target construction.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Try a few more arrangements before checking, so the 'only one' claim is actually tested.

explanationVariants: For 5, 7, 11: 5 + 7 = 12 > 11, so the sides reach and one triangle exists.
Check the two shorter sides against the longest: their sum must exceed it.

widget.prompt: Which set of side lengths CAN form a triangle?

options.feedback: 5 + 7 = 12, which is more than 11 — the short sides reach across and meet.
3 + 4 = 7, less than 9. The sides fall short.
1 + 6 = 7, less than 8. The shortest side is far too small to help.

steps.body: The boundary case is the interesting one.
explanationVariants: 4 + 6 = 10, exactly the third side, so the sides lie flat along it and enclose no area — no triangle.
Equality is the failure boundary: the sides just touch in a straight line rather than meeting above it.
hints: Add the two shorter sides and compare with the longest.
4 + 6 = 10, which is exactly 10 — not more than it.
When the sum EQUALS the third side, the sides lie flat in a straight line, so no triangle is formed.

widget.prompt: How many triangles have sides 4, 6 and 10?

options.label: None
options.feedback: 4 + 6 = 10 exactly. The two sides lie flat along the third in a straight line, enclosing no area at all.

options.label: Exactly one
options.feedback: The sides must be strictly longer than the third to meet above it. Here they only just reach, lying flat.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: Fixed side lengths never give two triangles — that comes from ambiguous angle conditions.

options.label: Infinitely many
options.feedback: The lengths are fixed, so the size is fixed. Here they cannot form a triangle at all.

steps.body: Three lengths, and the question of whether they leave a choice.
takeaways: Three fixed sides (SSS) determine exactly one triangle, up to flips and turns.
Two sides with the angle BETWEEN them (SAS) also determine exactly one.
The two shorter sides must together exceed the longest, or no triangle exists at all.
steps.teaser: Next: the conditions that leave a choice — two triangles, or infinitely many.

concept.body: Rewind. Three side lengths build a triangle only when the two shorter ones together **exceed** the longest. 3 and 4 total 7, which is more than 5, so 3-4-5 works.

explanationVariants: 2 + 4 = 6, which is less than 9, so the sides cannot reach.
The two shorter sides fall short of the longest, so no triangle forms.

widget.prompt: Can sides 2, 4 and 9 form a triangle?

options.label: No
options.feedback: 2 + 4 = 6, which is less than 9 — the short sides never meet.

options.label: Yes, exactly one
options.feedback: Compare 2 + 4 with 9: six cannot span nine.

options.label: Yes, two of them
options.feedback: Three fixed sides never give two triangles, and these cannot even make one.
